rationale: Use one Ridge model for all drugs as before, but pick each drug's own penalty with efficient leave-one-out GCV (RidgeCV with alpha_per_target) instead of a fixed alpha=5000. Expression predicts some drugs well (targeted oncology agents) and others hardly at all (many non-oncology repurposing compounds), so the strong-signal drugs should get less shrinkage and the weak, noisy ones more.

A large share of drug sensitivity in PRISM follows tissue lineage. With alpha=5000, the ridge model shrinks those lineage signals heavily when they are spread over thousands of genes. This change first fits a per-drug lineage mean from the training lines, pulled toward the drug's overall mean in proportion to how few lines that lineage has (shrinkage). The expression ridge then models only what is left over after that lineage mean, and the two parts are added at prediction time.

Many PRISM drugs carry only weak, noisy signal on their own, but drug responses are strongly correlated with each other (general cytotoxicity, shared mechanism of action, lineage axes). This change keeps the same ridge but makes it reduced-rank: the ridge predictions are projected onto the top-k drug-response components of the fitted values, so weak drugs borrow strength from shared response axes. k is chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold.

The reduced-rank step runs the SVD on raw AUC values, so the shared response axes are dominated by the drugs with the largest AUC variance. This change z-scores each drug's AUC (using training-fold mean and SD, with missing values filled as 0) before the ridge and the projection, then transforms the predictions back. Every drug then counts equally when the shared axes are built. The ridge itself is fit separately per drug with one alpha, so per-drug Pearson is unchanged before projection and only the shared-axis estimate changes.
